newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Fighting spreads to Zaire's Shaba province.
newsitem.headline: Fighting spreads to Zaire's Shaba province.

text.p: Rebel fighting has spread to the north of Zaire's mineral-producing Shaba province with the army battling to hold on to the lake-side town of Kalemie, a senior defence ministry official said in Kinshasa on Monday.

"Since last night there has been heavy fighting in the northern part of Kalemie," the official told Reuters. "The FAZ (Zaire army) controls it but reinforcements are having to be sent in from the military base at Kamina."

Military sources in the region said rebels had already seized Kalemie, birthplace of guerrilla leader Laurent Kabila. They said the town fell on Sunday after heavy fighting between government troops and Kabila's Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (ADFL).
Kinshasa's Soft daily said on Monday government soldiers short of supplies had made a tactical withdrawal from Kalemie.
The town, about 800 km (500 miles) on a crumbling road to the provincial capital Lubumbashi, is still a long way away from Shaba's copper and cobalt mining heartland.

But military and political sources said even a tiny foothold on a corner of Shaba could raise the chances of the province's rebellious leaders siding with the guerrillas. That would minimise the need for rebels to fight their way through.
Kalemie is also on an important railway line that runs through Lubumbashi all the way to South Africa and is a major trading post with neighbouring Tanzania across Lake Tanganyika.
Rebel control of Kalemie could threaten Zaire's important military base at Kamina where government forces would normally be sent to Lubumbashi by rail.
The defence official added that rebels had taken the town of Watsa in Upper Zaire, north of Kalemie but that foreign mercenaries backing the army were defending the airport there.
Spreading war threatens a new humanitarian crisis in eastern Zaire where about 600,000 refugees from the Hutu tribe are trapped in equatorial forests, aid officials say.
Most fled earlier fighting last year. Church sources said much of the local population in Upper Zaire had also dispersed into the bush, leaving whole towns and vilages empty.
Zaire accuses Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi of fighting along with ethnic Tutsis who launched an armed rebellion last October and have since seized several towns in eastern Zaire.

Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko Mobutu, who has been convalescing in France from prostate cancer surgery, arrived in Morocco for a three-day visit and talks with long-time ally King Hassan expected to centre on the fighting.

Moroccan troops helped put down a 1977 secessionist uprising in Shaba after Zairean forces were overwhelmed. Moroccan forces also relieved French and Belgian paratroops backing Zairean authorities in the mining town of Kolwezi the following year.
Military sources say the Zaire government's much-touted counter-offensive launched only two weeks ago had been hampered by the lack of large airstrips in their control.
Cargo planes capable of handling sufficient supplies of munitions and weaponry for a major offensive are unable for now to reach troops close to the several fronts, they said.

The main military base is at Kisangani airport where most of Zaire's airborne weaponry including helicopters and Italian fighter jets, is stationed. Important airports in Goma, Bukavu and Bunia are under rebel control.

Recently acquired MI combat helicopters from Russia, used in the Chechen war, cannot reach rebel strongholds hundreds of kilometres from Kisangani without having to return to refuel, the military sources said.
